Press Release:


Nepal Earthquake
The world has rushed to the aid of a country in mourning as the death toll mounts following Nepal’s 7.8 magnitude earthquake. The quake has wreaked havoc on the region’s ancient infrastructure and iconic mountain ranges. As South African relief workers and doctors return from Nepal, Carte Blanche hears first-hand accounts of this devastating natural disaster.


Script:


NEPAL EARTHQUAKE

V/O: It was the weekend in Kathmandu, just before midday on Saturday the 25th of April when the earth began to move. A violent earthquake measuring 7.8 on the Richter scale would bring the bustling capital city to a standstill, and spell death and destruction for thousands of locals and tourists.
Eileen: It’s the most terrifying thing I’ve ever been through in my life, because of the helplessness and the lack of control.
Bongani link:
Nepal is something of an adventure tourism mecca, that’s why when the earthquake struck there were people there from all over the world, including South Africans.
V/O: Eileen Botha and Tony Burisch were in a group of friends who’d spent 2 weeks trekking and white water rafting in Nepal. It was their last day and they were doing some last minute shopping in Kathmandu.
Eileen: And then everything started going like this: the concrete, the tarmac was going like this and it took a while to realize. I thought what on earth’s going on here? You just think to yourself this cant be? An earthquake? This wasn’t on my bucket list.
V/O: They ran through the streets to the nearest open space which was an empty building site.
Eileen: But there were some steel rods that had been sunk I suppose for I suppose for concrete posts, and they were swaying like trees, like this. It was just absolute disbelief, you think this can’t be happening.
Tony: For the next 24 hours there were shock waves every now and again. It was scary, because you didn’t know if the shock waves are even going to get more and stronger.
Eileen: We were hanging onto one another. I don’t think I’ve ever prayed so hard in my life.
V/O: After 2.5 hours they made their way to the hotel and were driven to the airport.
Eileen: We saw the devastation and all the buildings, and everybody out in the open and in the parks away from the building trying to keep safe.
V/O: But the airport was closed, with thousands of people queuing for a flight out of the country.
Eileen: We had a little space in our corner and we set up in our corner and stayed there for 30 hours.
V/O: What they didn’t see was the destruction of all the historical monuments they’d visited only days before. Kathmandu’s Monkey Temple dates back to the 5th century and is considered the most sacred Buddhist pilgrimage site in Nepal.
The earthquake decimated these ancient shrines, and amidst the chaos one could see the clouds of dust from all the collapsing buildings in the valley below.
Durbar Square in Bakhtapur is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This plaza in front of the old royal palace is a popular tourist attraction, but on the 25th of April the earthquake demolished the 500 year-old temples.
Kathmandu’s Durbar Square stood for a thousand years. This impressive array of ancient palaces, courtyards and temples came crashing down 2 weeks ago.
Sfx: Woman crying & digging
Man: It’s a nightmare. I just need to find their bodies.
V/O: With emergency services completely overwhelmed by the destruction around the city, locals and tourists worked frantically to find survivors in the golden 72- hour period following the earthquake. But their equipment was hopelessly inadequate.
Hippie: Considering the tools were using and the manpower, it’s amazing.

V/O: Millions of people lost their homes and have had to rely on makeshift shelter, and food parcels for survival. Here they’re handing out small bags of cooking oil and noodles. With no sanitation and the monsoon season only weeks away, the risk of disease is ever-present.
Bongani link:
The initial images of the devastation that were beamed around the world were from Kathmandu, but the epicenter of the earthquake was in the mountains in the rural areas. And that’s where the trekkers were.
V/O: Eighteen schoolgirls from St Mary’s DSG in Pretoria were on a World Challenge tour to Nepal. The trip involved a strenuous hike and an outreach programme.
Erin: I think all of us wanted to grow as people and learn new life lessons.
Chloe: My goal was to get a closer bond with everyone and see all friendly faces in a different country.
V/O: On the day of the earthquake the girls were near Pokh’ra, about 150km from the epicenter.
Jess: We were on Day 4 of the hike. We’d just stopped for lunch after about 4 hours of hiking and we were having soup and the building started shaking, and we immediately evacuated the building and went and stood somewhere where nothing could fall on us.
Chelsey: I was really scared and I think with every little tremor –we just got so confused because we didn’t know what was going on.
Mampho: We were all the way up in the mountains and there could have been so much more damage than there actually was.
V/O: The girls had no cellphones, because part of the challenge was no communication with home.
Judite: For me it was the worst time, the first 5 hours because I actually thought my daughter was dead.
Anni: For me it was difficult not having heard from them until we knew. But in my heart I knew they were fine.
V/O: The girls had a lucky escape, but in other areas entire villages were wiped out.
Seismologists say the tectonic shockwave unleashed by the quake had the power of 20 thermonuclear weapons. A hundred miles east of the epicenter survivors from a border village were making their way towards the towns, looking for help.
Man: “Many people is dead there. All the way, is dead bodies - they’re smelling! There is no food, no tents, no medicine.”
V/O: In the Langtang valley South Africans Mike Sherman and Kate Ahrends were trekking when the quake struck.
Kate: The land kind of was vibrating violently, and the rocks were falling. And the more it shook , the bigger the rocks fell. And dust was rising up from the river and we just had no idea what to do. And we all ran together and kind of found part of the mountain that we could shelter ourselves in, but it really wasn’t much at all. And afterwards we looked at the area we were in and I think it was the only part of the road that was undamaged.
Mike: It was about 10 metres of road that was still there.
V/O: After six days in the mountains they were eventually rescued by a military chopper and flown to an army base in Kathmandu. From there they were put in touch with the Gift of the Givers.
Dr Qasim: A local Nepali picked them up and said “I know where the South Africans are”, contacted us, we went to meet them. I don’t know them at all, they don’t know me at all but we’re South Africans – that’s what unites us.
V/O: South African NGO Gift of the Givers was one of 4000 search & rescue teams from 34 countries that responded to the call for assistance.
Dr Qasim: It was slightly frustrating to be there because unfortunately we weren’t able to pull out anyone alive. We had running 5 hospitals with operating theatres in each of them. So we’ve done close to a hundred surgical procedures on patients who had a backlog for broken bones.
Dr Mariza: I’m a paediatric surgeon and we haven’t seen a lot of kids. Most of the cases were orthopaedic cases.
V/O: Nepal’s biggest attraction is Mount Everest, and April is the height of the climbing season. The earthquake caused a deadly avalanche that completely engulfed a packed Base Camp killing 18 people.
Sfx: Fuck! Fuck!
Ironically Base Camp was always considered a safe haven for climbers. Saray Khumalo was aiming to be the first black African woman to summit the world’s highest peak. She was between Camp 1 and Camp 2 when the quake struck.
Saray: The ground just started shaking and cracking. The most scary thing of my life, and my Sherpa hooked himself onto me. A moment after it just subsided, there were avalanches on both sides of the mountains approaching us. Again, very scary but my Sherpa was very calm. They’re Buddhists, so he started praying and I’m thinking to myself this is it. But after a moment it was all gone.
V/O: After 2 nights on the mountain they were airlifted back to an abandoned Base Camp, and Saray had to walk the rest of the way down. It was only the dead that were being ferried all the way back to Lukla airfield in the helicopters.
V/O: A third of Kathmandu’s population has fled the capital since the earthquake, but at the same time the injured are flooding in from the rural areas. The hospitals are overflowing and patients are housed under canvas.
Dr Qasim: Normally you have a spectrum of people injured. So you have your severe injured and your dead, and you have your moderately injured and then the minimal injured. Unfortunately in this earthquake there was no spectrum. It was either extremes. Those surviving had minor abrasions and minor injuries – the rest were all dead.
V/O The mortuaries are full, and dead bodies are piling up in hospital courtyards. The latest information puts the death toll at almost 9000.
Dr Qasim: In Nepal everyone is cremated. Now they are burning and cremating bodies everywhere. So you just see piles burning and it’s a continuous flame of sorrow.
Amrit Rai: People have been devastated, they have been shocked, but people of Nepal are very resilient. They are uniting at this moment of tragedy.
V/O: The Ambassador of Nepal, His Excellency Amrit Rai says his country needs all the help it can get.
Amrit: We still need medical supplies, we still need tents and tarpaulins and we still need food items. So individuals or organizations – whoever wants to come to Nepal at this time of tragedy, we will coordinate and we appreciate.
Eileen: I’m a nurse, I know life is short, but I didn’t think my life could be gone just like that. But you realize we’re very fragile. We’ve got to think about everything and be grateful: grateful, grateful, grateful and we are lucky.

Dr Qasim: A local Nepali picked them up and said “I know where the South Africans are”, contacted us, we went to meet them. I don’t know them at all, they don’t know me at all but we’re South Africans – that’s what unites us. V/O: South African NGO Gift of the Givers was one of 4000 search & rescue teams from 34 countries that responded to the call for assistance. Dr Qasim: It was slightly frustrating to be there because unfortunately we weren’t able to pull out anyone alive. We had running 5 hospitals with operating theatres in each of them. So we’ve done close to a hundred surgical procedures on patients who had a backlog for broken bones. Dr Mariza: I’m a paediatric surgeon and we haven’t seen a lot of kids. Most of the cases were orthopaedic cases. V/O: Nepal’s biggest attraction is Mount Everest, and April is the height of the climbing season. The earthquake caused a deadly avalanche that completely engulfed a packed Base Camp killing 18 people. Sfx: Fuck! Fuck! Ironically Base Camp was always considered a safe haven for climbers. Saray Khumalo was aiming to be the first black African woman to summit the world’s highest peak. She was between Camp 1 and Camp 2 when the quake struck. Saray: The ground just started shaking and cracking. The most scary thing of my life, and my Sherpa hooked himself onto me. A moment after it just subsided, there were avalanches on both sides of the mountains approaching us. Again, very scary but my Sherpa was very calm. They’re Buddhists, so he started praying and I’m thinking to myself this is it. But after a moment it was all gone. V/O: After 2 nights on the mountain they were airlifted back to an abandoned Base Camp, and Saray had to walk the rest of the way down. It was only the dead that were being ferried all the way back to Lukla airfield in the helicopters. V/O: A third of Kathmandu’s population has fled the capital since the earthquake, but at the same time the injured are flooding in from the rural areas. The hospitals are overflowing and patients are housed under canvas. Dr Qasim: Normally you have a spectrum of people injured. So you have your severe injured and your dead, and you have your moderately injured and then the minimal injured. Unfortunately in this earthquake there was no spectrum. It was either extremes. Those surviving had minor abrasions and minor injuries – the rest were all dead. V/O The mortuaries are full, and dead bodies are piling up in hospital courtyards. The latest information puts the death toll at almost 9000. Dr Qasim: In Nepal everyone is cremated. Now they are burning and cremating bodies everywhere. So you just see piles burning and it’s a continuous flame of sorrow. Amrit Rai: People have been devastated, they have been shocked, but people of Nepal are very resilient. They are uniting at this moment of tragedy. V/O: The Ambassador of Nepal, His Excellency Amrit Rai says his country needs all the help it can get. Amrit: We still need medical supplies, we still need tents and tarpaulins and we still need food items. So individuals or organizations – whoever wants to come to Nepal at this time of tragedy, we will coordinate and we appreciate. Eileen: I’m a nurse, I know life is short, but I didn’t think my life could be gone just like that. But you realize we’re very fragile. We’ve got to think about everything and be grateful: grateful, grateful, grateful and we are lucky.
